Description: The contract is to support DG CLIMA in the evaluation of the EU ETS and the review of certain elements due in 2026. An evaluation of the ETS Directive and the MSR Decision is required on the basis of the ‘evaluate first’ principle, i.e. before revisions of EU legislation. The evaluation will be limited to those issues which have not been subject, in part or in full, to major changes in the last revision of the ETS Directive (primarily free allocation for non-CBAM sectors, the Modernisation Fund, and the MSR), and any other elements that are maintained. Provisions that have been subject to major amendments should not be evaluated, as conclusions on their performance from 2015 (or 2021) cannot be addressed if other changes were made in the meantime. Four elements of the EU ETS are due for review in 2026: 1. Market Stability Reserve. For this review it will be necessary to: a. Analyse current market actors, hedging behaviour and stability risks in EU ETS b. Analyse options for changing the rules of the MSR (thresholds, intake rate) compared to baseline of continued policy c. Analyse, proportionate to political priority, more radical changes to MSR operation d. ex-ante analysis of ETS2 MSR operation 2. Negative emissions: how negative emissions resulting from greenhouse gases that are removed from the atmosphere and safely and permanently stored (BECCS and DACCS) could be accounted for and how those negative emissions could be covered by emissions trading , if appropriate, including a clear scope and strict criteria for such trading, and safeguards to ensure that such removals do not offset necessary emission reductions in accordance with the Climate Law. While reducing emissions remains the absolute priority in the coming years and decades in climate action, carbon removals will become increasingly important over time to deal with hardest to abate emissions and to reach negative emissions. 3. Accounting and double counting of non-permanent CCU: whether all greenhouse gas emissions covered by the ETS are effectively accounted for, and whether double counting is effectively avoided; in particular, regarding greenhouse gas emissions which are considered to have been captured and utilised in a product non-permanently. 4. Inclusion of municipal waste incineration (MWI) and other waste management processes: the feasibility of including municipal waste incineration installations in the EU ETS, with a view to their inclusion from 2028, and the possibility of including in the EU ETS other waste management processes, in particular landfills which create methane and nitrous oxide emissions. Regarding MWI, the report must to take into account: o the importance of all sectors contributing to emission reductions and potential diversion of waste towards disposal by landfilling in the Union and waste exports to third countries, and measures to prevent potential diversion of waste. o the effects on the internal market, o potential distortions of competition, o environmental integrity, o alignment with the objectives of the Waste Framework Directive, o robustness and accuracy of the monitoring and calculation of emissions. Topics 2, 3, and 4 are interconnected subjects that require an overall reassessment of how the ETS works. The three topics need to be seen in context of a CO2 value chain and move towards a circular carbon system in an ETS with a cap going to zero. For example, examining how the ETS treats embedded emissions in chemical products, the treatment of e-fuels and other non-permanent CCU products in case several waste management processes or MWI are included in the ETS, and the creation of a simple CO2 value chain in which removals may or may not be included in the ETS but part of the liability for reversals will be covered by the ETS in it's CCS activities. The contract will also require examining the interplay with environmental policies for both waste and the treatment of non-permanent CCU products.
